title: Lyra Therapeutics - Prompt Retention & Privacy Review

Share BYOK/KMS integration doc and HSM options
Draft short MSA clause on 'no training' commitment for Lyra's pilot
Schedule a follow-up technical deep-dive (SE-led) next week to review retention settings and demo audit logs

summary: Customer is evaluating Redwood for live inference of PHI-containing prompts in a clinical workflow. Main concerns: confirm no training on customer prompts/outputs, retention policy/auto-delete, BYOK/KMS support, audit logs for prompt access, SOC2/ISO evidence, HIPAA/BAA path. Redwood AE + SE clarified hosted vs Private options and immediate mitigations (short retention TTLs, redaction, dedicated nets). topics: Prompt & output retention windows and auto-delete
PII/PHI handling and HIPAA / BAA considerations
Encryption at rest / in transit, BYOK and HSM options
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-12 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 minutes | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood Security), Dr. Susan Park, Rajiv Menon (CISO), Ariana Gomez (PM), Evan Liu (Privacy Counsel)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're on the 16:00 UTC call, I'm Jordan from Redwood, with Maya and Liam, we'll run through security topics and answer questions. does that time still work for folks?
[00:08] Dr. Park: yes thanks. happy to be here. we'll mostly listen — we have some specific questions about prompt retention and whether data is used for training.
[00:15] Rajiv: hi, quick call out — Lyra is evaluating using the API in a clinical triage flow, there will be PHI in prompts. We need to understand retention and legal commitments, HIPAA scope, and whether Redwood ever trains on customer data.
[00:28] Maya: absolutely. high level we have three serving modes: hosted API, dedicated capacity, and private VPC/on-prem. each has different controls. today we'll cover default hosted behavior and the stronger guarantees for dedicated/private.
[00:39] Liam: and I'll jump in on encryption and audit logs. quick note, transcript may have some auto-caption noise, sorry for that.
[00:45] Ariana: can you say explicitly — does Redwood train models on customer prompts or outputs? we need a formal yes/no for procurement.
[00:53] Jordan: short answer: we do not train customer-provided prompts or outputs in our hosted models. to be precise, we don't add customer prompt or response data into training datasets for model weights. we can provide a written attestation for procurement.
[01:06] Evan: ok, procurement will want that attestation and also a clause in MSA. is there any telemetry or aggregated usage data that might be used to improve service-level models?
[01:16] Maya: we collect anonymized telemetry for runtime stability — e.g., error rates, latency percentiles, token counts. that telemetry is aggregated and cannot be traced back to a customer request. if you need, we can restrict telemetry collection for Dedicated/Private.
[01:28] Dr. Park: when you say 'anonymized' — is that irreversible? we have to be careful with small sample sizes from certain customers; re-identification is a concern.
[01:37] Liam: good point. our default telemetry strips request/response text before storage and retains only metadata and aggregated metrics. for customers with stricter requirements we recommend private deployment or dedicated and BYOK and we can turn off telemetry collection entirely, per contractual agreement.
[01:48] Rajiv: retention windows — what's the default retention for prompts and generated outputs on the hosted API?
[01:54] Maya: by default, we retain logs that include prompt and response text for 30 days to support debugging and abuse monitoring. however you can configure retention to as low as zero days for enterprise customers, or use dedicated/private where logs can be routed to your own S3 and TTL-managed, or even not stored.
[02:09] Jordan: to add, we have features to automatically redact or hash fields — e.g., PII detection hooks — that can remove or mask PHI before persisting logs. but that is something we'd want to work through in the SE deep-dive since detection has edge cases.
[02:22] Dr. Park: are redaction hooks client-side or server-side? we prefer client-side redaction to avoid sending PHI to the server at all.
[02:30] Maya: right now redaction is available as a server-side pre-processing filter that runs in the request pipeline. for the highest assurance you can perform redaction on your side before sending, and we support field-level inputs so you can pass in non-sensitive IDs instead. for dedicated/private we can also ship a pre-request plugin to run in your VPC.
[02:45] Evan: on HIPAA and BAA — what's Redwood's stance? do you sign BAAs?
[02:51] Jordan: we do sign BAAs with qualifying customers. There is an enterprise onboarding process and some minimum requirements (dedicated capacity or private deployment depending on the use case). we'll share our BAA template and the security questionnaire responses after the call.
[03:03] Rajiv: KMS / BYOK — can we bring our own keys and have the keys never leave our account?
[03:09] Liam: yes, we support BYOK for certain deployment modes. For hosted, we do a managed KMS with option for customer-managed keys where keys are in AWS KMS or GCP KMS under your account and Redwood gets cryptographic access via an IAM role. for an on-prem HSM option we can discuss HSM-backed keys and attestations.
[03:25] Maya: practical note: BYOK for the model cache encryption and persistent log storage is supported. ephemeral compute still needs keys for runtime — we can tie in an HSM for key unwrap on the node and then zeroize — the specifics depend on dedicated vs private.
[03:38] Dr. Park: do you surface key-rotation events and key-use audit logs to the customer?
[03:42] Liam: we can surface key-usage logs to your cloud account if keys are in your KMS. we also store an audit trail of key reference operations in our audit log and can export that to your SIEM.
[03:51] Ariana: audit logs — level of granularity? we need full traceability: who queried what prompt, who accessed logs, retention of audit logs, and immutable export for compliance.
[04:00] Maya: our audit logs include request id, timestamp, which tenant, calling principal (API key or SSO user), route, model variant, and a pointer to the stored artifact. you can configure retention and export to your S3 or syslog. immutable export requires an append-only store on your side; we can push there.
[04:17] Rajiv: what about RBAC / SSO integration — we use Okta and want SCIM provisioning and SAML SSO.
[04:24] Jordan: full SSO/SAML and SCIM provisioning are supported. you can map roles to access control: who can create API keys, who can change retention settings, who can download logs.
[04:35] Evan: is there object-level access control for prompts/records? e.g., separate teams within Lyra who can access different sets of prompts?
[04:42] Maya: we support tenant-level RBAC out of the box. object-level ACLs are available in dedicated/private variants via route-level permissions and token scoping. we'd plan to show this in the SE demo — show role changes and the resulting permission enforcement.
[04:56] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[05:00] Maya: quick aside on training language again — many vendors say 'we don't use customer content to train base models' but then they have marketplace or fine-tuning datasets. Redwood's policy: no customer data is used for model training of shared models, and we do not surface customer prompts into our fine-tune pipeline. for customers who want private fine-tuning we support an isolated pipeline but that requires explicit opt-in and contractual terms.
[05:23] Dr. Park: if we opt into private fine-tune with our own data, will the fine-tuned model be accessible only to us?
[05:28] Maya: yes, private fine-tune artifacts are isolated to your tenant and never merged into public models. we can provide architecture docs for that flow.
[05:35] Rajiv: log deletions — if we request deletion of historic prompts, can you guarantee complete deletion across backups and any indexes?
[05:42] Liam: we have a documented deletion lifecycle. for hosted we delete primary copies and scrub indexes within a defined window, but backups might have longer retention for disaster recovery. for contractual deletions we can negotiate deletion windows and can arrange for snapshots to be purged from backups within a negotiated SLA, or choose dedicated/private to avoid the shared backup issue.
[05:58] Jordan: in practice for high-assurance customers we combine BYOK + dedicated capacity + agreed backup purge windows in the contract.
[06:06] Ariana: for the pilot we want to keep retention to 24 hours for prompts and outputs and disable telemetry. is that possible?
[06:11] Maya: yes — for a pilot we can set a short TTL (24 hours), disable request/response logging for storing, and still keep basic runtime metrics. we will run an SE checklist to ensure nothing is persisted beyond that.
[06:23] Evan: can you provide a signed attestation that during the pilot Redwood will not use any prompts or outputs for training, will delete logs per the 24-hour TTL, and will not export any prompt content to external analytics?
[06:33] Jordan: yes we can produce an attestation memo and include it as an addendum for the pilot. procurement will want to see it.
[06:39] Rajiv: threat model question — insider access: how many Redwood employees can access raw prompts in hosted environment and under what controls?
[06:47] Liam: strict need-to-know. access to raw prompt text is audited and gated. we have role-based escalation, and all access to production logs goes through a privileged access review flow with 4-eye approval and short lived access. every access event is logged. we can show our internal policy redacted if needed.
[07:02] Dr. Park: do you do background checks or certifications on folks who have privileged access?
[07:06] Liam: yes, we do background checks for employees with privileged access and we have mandatory NDA and least-privilege. we also provide a SOC2 control mapping which lists the controls around privileged access.
[07:16] Maya: quick note on model fallbacks and routing — sometimes systems route to a fallback model for latency; we'd want to ensure fallback variants have the same no-training guarantees and retention policies. we can bind a policy to the route to ensure consistent handling.
[07:29] Ariana: good, we want that in writing.
[07:33] Jordan: noted. we'll include a routing/route policy example in the follow-up.
[07:38] Speaker 2: (whisper)
[07:42] Maya: another practical suggestion: use client-side identifiers instead of PII in prompts, e.g., patient_id:12345, and keep PHI in your EHR system. call the model with a non-identifying context and have mapping happen back in your environment. reduces exposure.
[07:58] Dr. Park: that is our preferred approach — we built a tokenization layer to mask PHI. we just wanted the assurance that if some PHI slips into logs, retention and deletion are enforceable.
[08:08] Liam: understood. we will include the retention and deletion workflow diagram in the packet; shows how objects are removed from primary stores, index scrubbing, and backup purge timelines.
[08:18] Rajiv: what about data residency? some of our data must remain in eu-west-1. do you support region pinning for hosted?
[08:25] Maya: yes, region pinning is supported for enterprise — requests from eu-region can be routed to eu-hosted clusters. for strict residency we recommend Dedicated in the target region or Private where you control the data plane.
[08:37] Ariana: on audit logs we want alerts when any user exports raw prompts. can you surface real-time alerts?
[08:43] Liam: yes, we have audit event hooks and can push to webhook/SIEM for real-time alerting on specific action types like 'export:raw_prompt' or 'download:log'.
[08:53] Evan: cryptographic proof of deletion — do you support signed deletion receipts? some pharm clients like to get an auditable deletion token.
[08:59] Maya: we can generate deletion receipts for primary store operations; for backups, we need contractual windows. we can provide signed receipts for key operations and for purge jobs. we'll confirm the exact format.
[09:10] Dr. Park: are you SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 certified?
[09:14] Jordan: we are SOC2 Type II compliant and have ISO27001 certification; I'll attach the reports and condensed control mappings after the call.
[09:22] Rajiv: is there any custom engineering effort required to meet our 24-hour TTL pilot?
[09:27] Maya: minimal configuration and an SE checklist. We'll set up route and tenant-level ttl and confirm telemetry toggles. no heavy dev effort.
[09:35] Speaker 3: (phone echo)
[09:38] Jordan: ok let's go through hypothetical flow quick — a provider enters a clinical note with PHI, the client-side service tokenizes PHI and sends a sanitized prompt; the response streams back and you rehydrate locally. if somebody mistakenly sends raw PHI, the request would hit the pre-processing redactor and either mask or drop the field depending on policy.
[09:59] Dr. Park: sounds good. if the redactor fails we need an alert. can you trigger an incident if PHI passes the filter?
[10:05] Liam: yes we can create detection alerts for PHI-detection-failures and create an SRE incident channel.
[10:11] Ariana: any SLAs on forensic log exports for legal hold?
[10:15] Jordan: we can support forensic exports within an agreed SLA — typically 48-72 hours for export of raw logs when contractual, but can be negotiated for enterprise customers.
[10:26] Rajiv: on privacy-preserving analytics — if you run aggregated usage models, will any differential privacy or noise injection be applied?
[10:33] Maya: we don't currently apply DP by default. If you need DP guarantees we can discuss a custom analytics pipeline that uses differential privacy for aggregated telemetry.
[10:43] Evan: what's the path for a legal HOLD — if regulators request data preservation, how does Redwood handle an incoming legal hold for a tenant?
[10:51] Liam: we have a legal hold workflow: freeze deletion lifecycle for the affected objects, snapshot into an escrowed, encrypted store, and record the hold in the audit log. details again are contractual.
[11:03] Dr. Park: for our pilots we need a simple readout: 1) attestation of no-training on prompts/outputs, 2) 24-hour retention enforced, 3) BYOK option documented, 4) SOC2/ISO docs.
[11:16] Jordan: that's doable. we'll attach the artifacts and propose dates for the follow-up SE demo.
[11:22] Maya: i'll take point on the demo checklist and show retention toggles, audit log exports, and SSO role changes.
[11:28] Rajiv: please also confirm that fallback models used for latency will inherit retention and no-training policy.
[11:33] Liam: yes, we'll include a route policy example.
[11:37] Jordan: any remaining questions?
[11:39] Ariana: one last quick item — encryption at rest algorithms? AES-256?
[11:43] Liam: AES-256-GCM for at-rest; TLS1.3 in transit. key wrapping uses RSA-3072 or KMS-managed keys depending on provider.
[11:51] Dr. Park: great. thanks all.
[11:53] Jordan: recap of next steps: SOC2 + ISO docs, BYOK/KMS integration doc, legal attestation for no-training and 24h TTL, SE deep-dive demo. we'll shoot calendar invites for next week.
[12:06] Rajiv: thanks, we'll review and Evan will send legal redlines.
[12:10] Evan: will do. thanks everyone.

End meeting.
